questions.q: In the Movies dataset, what does one movie's 5-D vector contain?
options: The ratings it received from 5 different users
The 5 principal components of the movie
questions.explain: Each movie is described by the ratings (1–5) given by the same 5 users, so every movie lives in the same 5-D rating space.

questions.q: What is PCA used for on this page?
options: To squeeze high-dimensional vectors (5-D, 50-D, 784-D) down to 3-D so we can plot them
To add more dimensions to the data
To label each point with its group
questions.explain: PCA finds 3 directions that keep as much variation as possible, so similar items still land near each other in the 3-D plot.

questions.q: Why does each dataset get its **own** PCA instead of plotting movies, words and images in one space?
options: Each kind of data has its own number of dimensions and its axes measure different things
PCA can only handle 10 points at a time
All three would land on exactly the same point
Words cannot be represented as vectors
questions.explain: A 5-D rating vector and a 784-D pixel vector are not comparable — the page notes that comparing a movie point with a word point would be meaningless.

questions.q: In the 3-D plots, "king" sits near "queen" and action movies cluster together. What does that closeness mean?
options: PCA always puts labels in alphabetical order
Nothing — the positions are chosen by hand
They have the same number of dimensions as everything else, so position is random
Their vectors are similar, which is exactly what AI models exploit
questions.explain: Similar items have similar vectors, so they end up close together; models use that geometric closeness to find related items.
